strict_mean_counterexample.definition: B_alpha = inf{ b >= 0 : P(valid distinct completion by deadline D using total cost <= b) >= alpha }. This is a pathwise total-budget objective, distinct from mu = E[C].

strict_mean_counterexample.conclusion: At b=mu=5/2, Law A succeeds with probability only 1/4, below 1/2. Law B has the identical mu but half-success budget 1. Therefore substituting an expected-cost number for a fixed-confidence hard-cap endpoint is unsound without a conversion theorem.
scope_limits: These are finite declared laws, not an attack, native miner measurement, W1 cost bound or physical/quantum resource claim.
The lower-bound/optimum interpretation is relative only to the specified single-algorithm finite experiment.

If the target objective minimizes unconditional expected cost over all algorithms whose success probability is at least alpha, and has no incompatible deadline or scope restriction, a legal almost-sure algorithm is in that class and its mean can be an upper bound. It is still not a lower bound.

For a nonnegative almost-sure-completing cost with known mean mu, Markov can give a sufficient resource cap mu/(1-alpha) after an explicit truncation construction; this does not automatically establish the time deadline, legality of interruption, or all-strategy lower bound.
